extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, engineers, technical practitioners, and informed general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging scientific books, short reports, letters, and observational notes across disciplines (metallurgy, horticulture, astronomy, medicine, zoology, meteorology). Emphasises author qualifications, experimental grounding, completeness of coverage, clarity, and quality of illustrations and data reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' practical qualifications and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors possess special qualifications for the work they have undertaken (e.g., held positions such as foundry foreman, Carnegie research medallist, Associate of the Royal School of Mines) and have personally followed the operations they describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer authors who combine scientific training with practical experience; direct, first-hand experience under normal foundry and experimental laboratory conditions strengthens authority and usefulness to practitioners and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and comprehensiveness of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage should match the title and claimed scope (e.g., a work titled 'General Foundry Practice' should comprehensively treat foundry practice rather than be narrowly confined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear table of contents/heads (examples listed: moulding sands, foundry tools, cores, chill casting, metals other than iron, alloys, mechanical testing, foundry management). Note and justify any major omissions or narrow focus relative to the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations and production quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be carefully chosen and well printed (example: 246 illustrations carefully chosen; letterpress exceptionally well printed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality figures and good printing materially increase a work's value—report number, selection rationale, and reproduction quality; include plates/photographs where they aid identification or demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific grounding and experimental validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical knowledge should be built on experiment and theories tested by further experiment; practical remedies should be devised and tested scientifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise methods founded on experiment rather than guesswork (example: mixing by analysis replacing mixing by fracture/guesswork). Authors should document experiments and indicate how practice follows from tested theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of relevant subtopics and explicit mention of omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful technical book should include important related processes and subtopics (e.g., bronze casting methods, plaster moulds, galvanising, nickel‑plating, lacquering, porcelain enamelling, repair techniques, pattern making), or explicitly state why they are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either include practical treatments of commonly used adjacent processes or acknowledge and justify their absence; note when distinct trades (e.g., pattern making) are excluded but would nonetheless benefit the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, editorial quality, and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should be unusually free from typographical and other errors, with sound arrangement of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal typos, clear organization, and logical sequencing are expected; comment on editorial standards and layout as part of assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility for intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should provide information useful for its primary audience (students, foundry managers, foremen, amateurs), including practical methods, measurements, and managerial guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the level of detail and topics (e.g., high-temperature measurement, mixing by analysis, management) match the needs of students and practitioners; note opportunities to extend practical content for particular readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial enthusiasm and observational insight (horticulture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enthusiasm and a keen eye for artistic setting and arrangement make horticultural writing stimulating and valuable to amateurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the author's enthusiasm, aesthetic sense, and ability to convey practical and artistic garden-composition advice that amateurs can apply to poor soils or constrained sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical horticultural guidance and species-specific advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful horticultural books include lengthy, organised choices of species/varieties (e.g., roses arranged by colour groups), and practical methods (e.g., growing bulbs in peat fibre in bowls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lists of varieties, species suitability for local soils, hands-on cultivation tips, and whether recommended methods are practical and clearly described for amateurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic presentation and accessibility to amateurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of artistic combinations and planting arrangements should be accessible and instructive for non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how well the author translates aesthetic ideas into practical combinations readers can replicate; note illustrative examples from the author's own and friends' gardens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility for beginners and general readers (astronomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work that treats apparent movements, brightest stars, and introductory problems should appeal to beginners and general readers as well as to astronomers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of exposition for non-specialists, avoidance of excessive jargon, and provision of basic conceptual context (e.g., seasonal apparitions, diurnal paths, colour, and simple physical notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical identification aids (stars/constellations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of concise descriptive characteristics and frequent diagrams aids recognition of individual stars and constellations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate usefulness of diagrams and the sufficiency of characteristic notes for field identification; check whether the arrangement helps readers to 'be au fait' with star identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical synthesis and context (medical texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical/historical accounts should place practices (e.g., Lister's antiseptic methods) in chronological context and trace evolution of techniques and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the lectures/book properly document the development of methods, referencing primary experiments and subsequent modifications (carbolic acid, putty dressings, corrosive sublimate, cyanide gauzes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical appraisal of clinical practices and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should state and defend clinical judgments (example: 'no mere dressing with dry sterilised wool or gauze, apart from microbicidal solutions, will suffice to prevent suppuration in dirty wounds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the strength and evidence for prescriptive claims; note controversial stances and whether they are supported by historical or experimental data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise observational data reporting (meteors, phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational reports should include precise times, positions (RA/Dec or bearing), magnitudes, counts, velocities, and lengths of visible course (example: positions of Draconic radiant across years, meteor observed at specific time and coordinates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear tabulation of positional data, times, brightness estimates, and any derived quantities to facilitate later comparison and analysis by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent observations and corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports are strengthened by independent observations from different locations and observers (examples: same meteor recorded at Bristol and Stockport; requests for further descriptions to determine real course).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage collection of corroborating accounts and cross-referencing observer notes to refine trajectories and origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of physical specimens and environmental measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, submit physical specimens (e.g., wire specimens) and contemporaneous environmental readings (dry bulb, wet bulb, barometer, wind) with reports of unusual events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specimens and meteorological/contextual data permit quantitative analysis and help constrain interpretations (e.g., whether tin melted but wire not fused).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative estimation and physical calculations from observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should attempt quantitative estimates where appropriate, using stated assumptions (example: estimating heat energy limits from melted tin and assumed specific heat, producing energy bounds in ergs and relating to mass uplift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear statement of assumptions, intermediate steps, units, and sensitivity to assumptions; such calculations should be used to bracket plausible ranges rather than present unwarranted precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental tests of taxonomic hypotheses (breeding evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of controlled breeding experiments (placing two wild species together and observing progeny) to test hypotheses about the origin of domestic forms (example: cross of Felis sylvestris and Felis ocreata producing typical striped tabby kittens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental breeding with documented parentage and offspring phenotypes is strong evidence for origin hypotheses; report provenance and breeding conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative morphological identification against established figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossil/specimen identification should be supported by close comparison with established figures and venation/structural details (example: match to figures in Wellcome Laboratories report; note venation differences that may be generic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and compare with type figures and prior descriptions; explicitly note congruences and small differences and discuss their possible taxonomic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of theoretical prediction and experimental verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical work is most valuable when it makes clear predictions that can be later confirmed by experiment; both theoreticians and experimentalists are necessary for scientific progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value mathematical prediction awaiting confirmatory facts as high achievement; discourage dismissal of theory by the public and encourage recruitment of experimentalists to test predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear communication to non-specialists to avoid misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and speakers should take care that phrases and expressions do not lend themselves to damaging public misunderstanding (example: avoiding terms like 'chemistry of phantoms' or 'exuberance of mathematical speculation' when addressing a wider audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing broader audiences, clarify scope and intent of cautions; frame specialist debates so they cannot be misread as wholesale criticism of entire subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and correspondence policy for letters/manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by correspondents; will not undertake to return or correspond about rejected manuscripts; no notice taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and correspondents should avoid anonymity and should not expect returned manuscripts or individual correspondence about rejections; follow stated submission policies.
